pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, with the trade-off named in each; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Your authentication middleware rejects nobody — an unknown cookie just leaves an anonymous subject. Why is that better than a 401 right there, and where does the 401 come from instead?
expected_points: authentication answers who; authorization answers whether — separate concerns, separate failures
every refusal comes out of one gate, so there is one place to audit and one place to log
401 for anonymous and 403 for denied are decided together, from the same decision function
a middleware that rejected would also have to know which routes are public

questions.prompt: Name the four places your service consults the policy, and say what each can decide that the others cannot. Why is that still one enforcement point?
expected_points: route gate: role vs action, before any handler runs
object check in the handler: ownership, because only the handler has the row
listing scope: a predicate in the query rather than a filter over loaded rows
stream filter: per event, because the hub knows nothing about who may see what
one function interprets the rules; only the invocation is distributed

questions.prompt: Why does the listing scope ask the policy a question instead of saying "auditors and admins see everything"?
expected_points: a role literal is a second copy of the access-control model
narrowing the rule table would silently leave the listing wide open
deriving it means one edit reaches the gate, the object check, the listing and the stream
it is testable by swapping the rule table and watching the scope follow

questions.prompt: In your create handler, which writes share a transaction and which one deliberately does not? Walk through a crash at the worst moment for each ordering.
expected_points: task row and job row commit together — no ordering of two systems survives a crash
the event is published after the commit, because a transaction can roll back and a screen cannot
publishing first means clients see a task that never existed, with no correction coming
the accepted gap: a crash between commit and publish loses an announcement, recovered by refresh or Last-Event-ID replay

questions.prompt: The queue redelivers a notify job whose work already committed. Trace what happens, and say why the dedup marker lives in the pool rather than in each handler.
expected_points: the pool inserts the processed marker on the same transaction it hands the handler, and it reports first-vs-duplicate
a duplicate never reaches the handler: no second row, and no events for the pool to publish
guarding only the database write would still publish, so the owner is told twice
in the pool it is one rule no future job kind can forget; per handler it is a rule someone can omit invisibly
a marker written outside the transaction would turn the next retry into a silent skip
at-least-once is the contract, not a bug to fix

questions.prompt: Defend your middleware order. Why is the rate limiter on the side of authentication that it is, and what does that cost you?
expected_points: security headers outermost so 401s, 403s and 429s carry them too
limiting per account beats limiting per address (NAT, roaming clients, cheap IPv6 ranges)
keying on an account requires identity to be established first
the cost is a session lookup on a refused request — a map read, against the body read and decode it still avoids
anonymous callers fall back to the address, which is what protects the login endpoint's password hashing

questions.prompt: The feed is cacheable and scoped by identity at the same time. Which headers make that safe, and what goes wrong without each?
expected_points: Cache-Control private (not public): no shared cache may store a per-user body
Vary: Cookie, or a cache keyed on the URL alone serves one session's page to another
the ETag still earns its place: a 304 with no body after the query and the authorization ran
caching belongs after the authorization decision, never in front of it

questions.prompt: An admin demotes a user who has three tabs open. What happens to those sessions in your design, and what would have happened with a stateless token?
expected_points: the target's sessions are destroyed, so the next request is anonymous
rotation is unavailable because a third party is applying the change
a signed token stays valid until it expires: nothing consults you when it is used
the standard mitigations (short access tokens plus a stored refresh token, denylists) rebuild the state tokens were sold as avoiding

questions.prompt: Justify SSE for this feature, then describe what in the product would make you switch to WebSockets and what that switch would cost in this codebase.
expected_points: traffic is one-way, so SSE is plain HTTP: the session cookie, middleware and observability all work unchanged
reconnection with Last-Event-ID is the browser's job, and eviction of a slow client is humane because of it
switch when the client becomes a peer — typing, collaboration, anything bidirectional
the cost: a dependency, an origin check with no preflight to lean on, reader/writer goroutine discipline, proxies that must handle upgrades
